title: Let's Debate LA's Screen Time Policy
author: Mike Petrilli
summary: Mike Petrilli uses LAUSD's newly adopted, comprehensive school screen time policy as a vehicle for a structured multi-perspective debate about what states and districts should actually do about student devices. The LAUSD policy — which bans screen time for pre-K through first grade, establishes grade-specific screen time limits up through high school, blocks YouTube and social media during the school day, and encourages reduced use of one-to-one devices in lower grades — is the first major screen time policy from a large district and provides a concrete object for evaluation. Petrilli convenes perspectives from education policy experts including Matt Yglesias, Dan Buck, Aimee Guidera, Tim Daly, and Rick Hess, as well as a special 'America 250' feature on NCLB and accountability from Bob Schwartz, Sara Allen, Kevin Huffman, and others. The article reflects the 'growing grassroots techlash' of 2026, in which phone bans have been followed by broader device restriction and screen time limit conversations. Rather than advocating a single position, Petrilli structures the piece as a genuine deliberation about evidence, values, and policy design, making it useful for school leaders and policymakers designing their own approaches.
points: LAUSD's policy is historically significant as the first comprehensive screen time policy from a major U.S. district, establishing grade-specific limits and a parental opt-in consent procedure — a model other large districts will evaluate.

The debate format surfacing multiple expert perspectives is itself a pedagogical move: there is no obvious 'right answer' to device policy, and the article models the kind of evidence-weighing and value-clarifying that good policy design requires.

The distinction between phone bans (targeting personal devices) and screen time policies (targeting all devices, including school-issued) is significant: LAUSD's approach implicates the district's own technology infrastructure investments.

The 'techlash' framing is useful: the article documents that concerns about screens in schools have moved from a fringe position to mainstream parent and educator pressure, shifting the political dynamics of reform.

The most practical takeaway for school leaders is a rubric for evaluation: any screen time policy should address what is being restricted, for whom, during what times, with what evidence base, and with what mechanism for parental involvement.
